IMG Worldwide, Inc., 360 F.Supp.2d 681, 687 (E.D.Pa.2005) (finding that a party’s engaging in motion practice and providing “substantial discovery” constituted waiver of contractual alternative dispute resolution provision).

See also generally Registrant’s Trial Brief, Sköld v. Galderma Labs., Inc., Cancellation No. 92052897 (T.T.A.B. Aug. 13, 2014), Docket No. 81. 18	The more significant problem with Love-joy’s argument that it had an “unfettered” right to redefine the House Accounts is that this interpretation would nullify portions of the Agreement’s termination provision. PL’s Opp. Br. at 17. Under the termination provision, the Agreement became effective January 1, 2004, and:
19	shall continue in force for a one (1) year period, and shall be automatically renewed for additional one (1) year periods thereafter unless terminated by written notice from either party to the other party not less than sixty (60) days prior to the end of the initial or any subsequent one (1) year term.

The Agreement also provides for termination by either party under certain additional circumstances, including (1) a change of 50% or more of the ownership of the other party; (2) the other party’s unreasonable and repeated failure to perform the terms and conditions of the Agreement; or (3) the other party’s filing of a bankruptcy petition. Id. Finally, the Agreement expressly contemplates that the parties could terminate the Agreement at any time by “mutual written agreement.” Id.
21	The termination provision, on its face, provides a comprehensive account of the ways in which the Agreement may be terminated. There is no indication in the Agreement that the parties contemplated that the House Accounts provision would constitute an additional means for terminating all of Lovejoy’s obligations under the Agreement. Under Lovejoy’s construction of the House Accounts provision, however, Lovejoy could, at any time and without Kamco’s consent, redefine every single account in Kamco’s territory as a House Account. This interpretation would allow Lovejoy to escape from all of its obligations under the Agreement and all of the restrictions in the termination provision.
22	This reading is inconsistent with Pennsylvania law, which, as noted above, forbids courts from “interpreting] one provision of a contract in a manner which results in another portion being annulled,” LJL Transp., 962 A.2d at 648 (citation omitted), and requires that “[t]he whole instrument ... be taken together in arriving at contractual intent,” Duquesne Univ., 777 A.2d at 429 (citation omitted). In other words, the “mutual” termination provision would never apply to Lovejoy.
23	Similarly, Lovejoy’s reading of the House Accounts provision would allow it to escape the effects of the 60 day notice requirement, under which the Agreement automatically renews for a full year unless either party provides notice of its intention to terminate the Agreement 60 days before the end of an annual term. 24	This court’s conclusion that Lovejoy’s reading of the House Accounts provision is inconsistent with the parties’ intent is reinforced by the fact that the Agreement contains a non-compete provision. Reading the House Accounts provision in this manner allows the termination provision to have its intended effect: If one of the parties wishes to put an end to its obligations to the other party, it must follow one of the enumerated ways of terminating the Agreement.

{"judgments": [
{"clause_id":"c001","reasoning_cat1":"Boilerplate integration/enumeration language, but it ends with an order-of-precedence rule ('If anything in the other Contract Documents is inconsistent with this Agreement, this Agreement shall govern') whose reach over addenda and exhibits is not spelled out.","reasoning_cat2":"That precedence rule sits against Supplementary Condition 1.2.1.1 (inconsistencies resolved by better quality/more stringent requirement per the Architect) and A201 1.2.1 (documents complementary), so a court could have to reconcile competing conflict rules.","prob_cat1":0.22,"prob_cat2":0.38},
{"clause_id":"c002","reasoning_cat1":"Short and standard: contractor fully executes the Work except as indicated to be others' responsibility; the exception is generic but conventional.","reasoning_cat2":"The First Addendum replaces this with Article 2 [Revised], so the operative text is elsewhere; no substantive conflict located.","prob_cat1":0.10,"prob_cat2":0.20},
{"clause_id":"c003","reasoning_cat1":"'Approximately the Fifteenth of July' is inherently imprecise for a commencement date that drives the Contract Time.","reasoning_cat2":"Addendum 4.1 [Revised] fixes July 15, 2002 'pending approval of permits', which both supersedes and qualifies this clause and interacts with A201 8.1.2's definition of the date of commencement.","prob_cat1":0.30,"prob_cat2":0.30},
{"clause_id":"c004","reasoning_cat1":"One definite sentence measuring Contract Time from the date of commencement; nothing to construe.","reasoning_cat2":"Consistent with A201 8.1.1-8.1.2 and Addendum 4.1; no conflict found.","prob_cat1":0.04,"prob_cat2":0.06},
{"clause_id":"c005","reasoning_cat1":"The completion deadline is stated in a partly blank/garbled fill-in ('five hundred ___ calendar days'), leaving the intended period uncertain on the face of the clause.","reasoning_cat2":"Addendum 4.3 [Revised] substitutes a fixed date of November 30, 2003, which does not obviously match any day count here, creating a potential inconsistency between the two completion terms.","prob_cat1":0.32,"prob_cat2":0.38},
{"clause_id":"c006","reasoning_cat1":"Defines the Contract Sum as Cost of the Work plus Fee; the terms are defined elsewhere and the sentence itself is definite.","reasoning_cat2":"It is the hinge of a cost-plus contract whose Guaranteed Maximum Price is filled in as 'N/A' (5.2.1) while Articles 8, 12 and 13 assume a GMP exists, so its operation as a whole is contestable.","prob_cat1":0.15,"prob_cat2":0.36},
{"clause_id":"c007","reasoning_cat1":"The Fee is stated in words and figures that appear not to match ('Three Hundred ... Thousand Dollars ($380,000)'), the classic mechanical defect, and it is unclear whether the fee is a lump sum or a rate.","reasoning_cat2":"Subparagraphs 12.1.7.3, 13.2.2 and 6.4 all speak of 'the rate stated in Subparagraph 5.1.2' or of equitable fee adjustment, which fits awkwardly with a single fixed sum.","prob_cat1":0.42,"prob_cat2":0.33},
{"clause_id":"c008","reasoning_cat1":"The guaranteed maximum figure is entered as 'N/A', so the clause purports to guarantee a maximum while stating none, and it then makes the Contractor bear costs exceeding that non-existent number.","reasoning_cat2":"Dozens of provisions (8.1.8, 10.2, 12.1.5, 12.1.6, 12.1.7.1-.2, 12.2.5, 13.2, 13.4) are built on a Guaranteed Maximum Price that this clause never supplies, a whole-instrument incoherence.","prob_cat1":0.52,"prob_cat2":0.62},
{"clause_id":"c009","reasoning_cat1":"A blank fill-in for alternates with only the AIA instructional note; nothing substantive to construe.","reasoning_cat2":"Refers to a Guaranteed Maximum Price that 5.2.1 leaves as 'N/A', but the blank makes the point academic.","prob_cat1":0.13,"prob_cat2":0.18},
{"clause_id":"c010","reasoning_cat1":"'Unit prices, if any, are as follows:' with nothing following; the clause is empty rather than ambiguous.","reasoning_cat2":"A201 4.3.9 and 7.3.3.2 contemplate unit prices 'stated in the Contract Documents'; the blank simply means they are not stated.","prob_cat1":0.10,"prob_cat2":0.14},
{"clause_id":"c011","reasoning_cat1":"Blank allowance fill-in; no operative words capable of two readings.","reasoning_cat2":"A201 3.8 governs allowances if any exist; the blank leaves nothing inconsistent, though Exhibits could be read as allowances.","prob_cat1":0.11,"prob_cat2":0.18},
